summary: Describes Opstat, a client-server model for retrieving operational statistics from network devices. Network administrators gather large amounts of raw data, and this model is meant to make that easier to handle. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for one computer to ask others for their score sheets so the person in charge can see how the network is doing.

subtitle: A client-server protocol for retrieving network statistics and performance data

tldr.problem: Network administrators collect gigabytes of performance data monthly but have no standard way to share that raw data among operators, service providers, and customers.
tldr.mechanism: Opstat defines a client-server model where clients authenticate to a statistics server, query available data with SELECT, then retrieve tagged datasets using GET, with servers managing access control and data consistency.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can retrieve network statistics through a common protocol, enabling better problem isolation and network planning across organizations.

facts.label: Main commands
facts.value: LOGIN, SELECT, LIST, STATUS, GET, EXIT

today: RFC 1856 is Informational and describes a model that was not widely adopted. It represents an early approach to network statistics sharing that influenced later standards for operational data exchange, though modern network management has evolved toward different protocols.

sections.title: The Data Sharing Problem
sections.content:
Network administrators gather enormous amounts of raw data about their networks—typically several megabytes to several gigabytes per month—tracking performance, utilization, and growth. This data is valuable for both immediate problem isolation and long-term network planning. However, in 1995, few tools existed for sharing this raw data among network operators or between a network service provider (NSP) and its customers.

Opstat addresses this gap by defining a model and protocol that Network Operation Centers (NOCs) and NSPs can use to share data among themselves and with customers in a structured, secure way.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks create lots of detailed statistics files. The people running them want to share these files with each other and with customers, but nobody had a standard procedure for doing it safely and reliably.

sections.title: The Client-Server Model
sections.content:
Opstat uses a classic client-server architecture. Each NOC or NSP installs a server that provides locally collected statistics. Clients connect to the server and use a query language to specify what they want: a network object, an interface, a metric, and a time period. The server processes the query and transmits the requested data over a reliable connection (typically TCP).

The client's role is to accept user requests, translate them into the Opstat protocol, send them to the server, wait for replies, and present the data to the user. The RFC does not specify how data should be presented—it could be graphed in an X window, rendered to PostScript for printing, or dumped as raw text.

The server's role is to accept connections, process commands, retrieve data from a local statistics database, manage user authentication, enforce access control, and return results. Each server maintains a configuration file listing authorized users and the data each user may access.
sections.plainLanguage: A server holds all the network records in one place. A client asks the server for specific records by describing what it wants. The server checks if the client is allowed to see it, then sends it over.

sections.title: The Protocol and Commands
sections.content:
Clients and servers communicate using six main commands:

  • LOGIN—authenticates the client. The server sends a challenge; the client responds with authentication data. Multiple authentication types are supported (password, S/Key, SecurID, or custom).
  • SELECT—marks data for retrieval. The client specifies a network, device, interface, variable name, time period, granularity (sampling interval), and optional aggregation (total or peak). The server returns a tag that identifies the selected dataset.
  • STATUS—shows the server's state and lists all tagged datasets with their sizes.
  • LIST—queries what data is available on the server using wildcards. For example, LIST * * * * * * * * * lists all networks; LIST netx rtry * * * * * * * lists all interfaces on a specific router.
  • GET—retrieves the data associated with a previously selected tag. The client specifies an encoding type (1404 is the standard; others may be supported).
  • EXIT—closes the connection.

All responses are three-digit numeric codes (like 910 for login success, 950 for GET data starting, 952 for GET complete). Error codes allow servers to communicate specific problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends commands like 'log me in', 'find data about this device', and 'give me that data'. The server responds with numbers that mean success or failure, and sends the data when asked.

sections.title: Server State Management
sections.content:
The RFC defines a state machine that servers must follow. After initialization, the server waits for a new connection. Upon receiving a connection, it requires the first command to be LOGIN. If LOGIN succeeds, the server enters a PROCESS state where it handles LIST, GET, STATUS, and SELECT commands. An EXIT command returns the server to the WAIT state.

If LOGIN fails or a syntax error occurs during LOGIN, the server immediately closes the connection without processing further commands. Once in PROCESS state, unrecognized commands are silently ignored, and the server will not interrupt a command in progress (such as a large GET) even if an EXIT is sent.

If the client closes the connection while the server is in PROCESS state, the server cleans up and returns to WAIT.
sections.plainLanguage: The server follows a simple sequence: wait for a client, ask them to log in, process their requests, and when they disconnect, go back to waiting.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The RFC recognizes that data sharing raises legal, ethical, and political concerns. Servers must implement access control to restrict what each user can access. The RFC recommends using either a configuration file listing allowed objects per user or file system permissions within the server's storage system.

Servers should reject default access to all data, strictly follow the state diagram to prevent bypasses, discard illegal control characters, verify that all data fits in input buffers to prevent overflow attacks, and test with arbitrary input strings. If a server executes external programs, it must verify no unexpected side-effects occur.

The RFC also notes that authentication via LOGIN should be strict, and one-time authentication (like S/Key) is strongly encouraged. Data returned from the server should ideally be encrypted to prevent sensitive information from being exposed by accident.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers must check that a client is allowed to see the data they're asking for, and they have to be careful not to let tricky input messages cause crashes or security holes.
